translations.literal: Lady Li, looking up to heaven, wailed: "I am a woman—if I cannot preserve my chastity, shall this hand be grasped by another!"
translations.idiomatic: Lady Li looked up to heaven and cried: "I am a woman! If I cannot keep my chastity intact, shall another man's hand seize mine?"

sentences.zh: 即引斧自斷其臂，見者為之嗟泣。

translations.literal: She immediately took up an axe and severed her own arm. Those who saw it sighed and wept for her.
translations.idiomatic: She seized an axe and cut off her arm. All who witnessed it wept.

sentences.zh: 開封尹聞之，白其事於朝，厚恤李氏而笞其主人。

translations.literal: When the Prefect of Kaifeng heard of this, he reported the matter to the court. Lady Li was generously compensated, and the innkeeper was beaten with the bamboo.
translations.idiomatic: The Kaifeng prefect reported the affair to court. Lady Li received generous relief, and the innkeeper was flogged.

sentences.zh: 嗚呼！

translations.literal: Alas!
translations.idiomatic: Alas!

sentences.zh: 士不自愛其身而忍恥以偷生者，聞李氏之風，宜少知愧哉！

translations.literal: Those scholars who do not cherish their own persons but endure shame to preserve their lives—on hearing Lady Li's example, they ought at least to know a little shame!
translations.idiomatic: Scholars who would rather live in dishonor than honor their own bodies should feel some shame when they hear what Lady Li did!

sentences.zh: 臣光曰：天地設位，聖人則之，以制禮立法，內有夫婦，外有君臣。

translations.literal: Your subject Guang remarks: Heaven and Earth establish their positions; the sages take them as models to form ritual and enact law. Within there are husband and wife; without there are ruler and minister.
translations.idiomatic: Sima Guang writes: Heaven and Earth set forth their stations, and sages take them as models to frame ritual and law—within, the bond of husband and wife; without, the bond of ruler and minister.

sentences.zh: 婦之從夫，終身不改；

translations.literal: A wife follows her husband and does not change for life;
translations.idiomatic: A wife follows one husband for life;

sentences.zh: 臣之事君，有死無貳。

translations.literal: a minister serves his ruler—death without doubling.
translations.idiomatic: a minister serves his ruler unto death without divided loyalty.

sentences.zh: 此人道之大倫也。

translations.literal: These are the great constants of human relations.
translations.idiomatic: These are the supreme bonds of human society.

sentences.zh: 苟或廢之，亂莫大焉！

translations.literal: If these are abandoned, there is no disorder greater!
translations.idiomatic: Once these are cast aside, chaos knows no limit.

sentences.zh: 范質稱馮道厚德稽古，宏才偉量，雖朝代遷貿，人無間言，屹若巨山，不可轉也。

translations.literal: Fan Zhi praised Feng Dao as deeply virtuous and steeped in antiquity, with grand talent and magnificent capacity—though dynasties changed and shifted, no one found fault with him; he stood like a great mountain, immovable.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Zhi hailed Feng Dao as a man of deep virtue steeped in antiquity, with grand talent and imposing stature—through regime after regime no fault was found in him; he stood like an immovable mountain.

sentences.zh: 臣愚以為正女不從二夫，忠臣不事二君。

translations.literal: Your subject, in his foolishness, holds that a chaste woman does not follow two husbands, and a loyal minister does not serve two rulers.
translations.idiomatic: I hold that a proper woman does not follow two husbands, and a loyal minister does not serve two rulers.

sentences.zh: 為女不正，雖復華色之美，織紝之巧，不足賢矣；

translations.literal: If a woman is not chaste, though her beauty be resplendent and her weaving and sewing skillful, she is not worthy to be called worthy;
translations.idiomatic: A woman who lacks propriety, for all her beauty and skill with the loom, is not admirable;

sentences.zh: 為臣不忠，雖復材智之多，治行之優，不足貴矣。

translations.literal: if a minister is not loyal, though he have abundant talent and wisdom and superior governance and conduct, he is not worthy to be prized.
translations.idiomatic: a disloyal minister, for all his talent and distinguished service, is not to be honored.

sentences.zh: 何則？

translations.literal: Why is this?
translations.idiomatic: Why?

sentences.zh: 大節已虧故也。

translations.literal: Because the great constant has already been breached.
translations.idiomatic: Because the supreme moral commitment has already been forfeited.

sentences.zh: 道之為相，歷五朝、八姓，若逆旅之視過客，朝為仇敵，暮為君臣，易面變辭，曾無愧怍，大節如此，雖有小善，庸足稱乎！

translations.literal: As chancellor, Dao served through five dynasties and eight royal surnames, like an innkeeper viewing passing guests: in the morning foes, by evening ruler and minister—changing countenance and altering words without a trace of shame. When the great constant is such as this, though there be minor virtues, what is there worth praising!
translations.idiomatic: As chancellor Feng Dao served five dynasties and eight royal houses, treating each as an innkeeper treats passing travelers—today's enemy, tomorrow's sovereign—changing face and changing words without a flicker of shame. With his great moral commitment so utterly void, what minor virtue could justify praise?

sentences.zh: 或以為自唐室之亡，群雄力爭，帝王興廢，遠者十餘年，近者四三年，雖有忠智，將若之何！

translations.literal: Some say that from the fall of the Tang house, contending warlords struggled for power; dynasties rose and fell—in the long term more than a decade, in the near term three or four years. Though one possessed loyalty and wisdom, what could one have done!
translations.idiomatic: Some argue that after Tang's fall, rival warlords battled for the throne, dynasties rising and falling every few years—decade-long struggles in some cases, three or four years in others—and ask what loyalty or wisdom could avail anyone.

sentences.zh: 當是之時，失臣節者非道一人，豈得獨罪道哉！

translations.literal: In those times, he who lost his integrity as a minister was not Feng Dao alone—how can Dao alone be blamed!
translations.idiomatic: In those days Feng Dao was hardly the only man who compromised his loyalty—why single him out for blame?

sentences.zh: 臣愚以為忠臣憂公如家，見危致命，君有過則強諫力爭，國敗亡則竭節致死。

translations.literal: Your subject, in his foolishness, holds that a loyal minister cares for the public weal as for his own family, gives his life when danger appears, remonstrates and strives strenuously when the ruler errs, and when the state collapses and perishes, exhausts his integrity and dies.
translations.idiomatic: A true loyal minister treats the realm as his own household, gives his life in danger, remonstrates forcefully when his ruler errs, and dies with honor when the state falls.

sentences.zh: 智士邦有道則見，邦無道則隱，或滅跡山林，或優遊下僚。

translations.literal: A wise man when the state is governed by the Way comes forth; when the state is not governed by the Way he withdraws—some vanishing into mountains and forests, some idly passing time in low offices.
translations.idiomatic: The wise serve when the state is well governed and withdraw when it is not—some vanishing into the mountains, others idling in minor posts.

sentences.zh: 今道尊寵則冠三師，權任則首諸相，國存則依違拱嘿，竊位素餐，國亡則圖全苟免，迎謁勸進。

translations.literal: Yet Feng Dao, in honor and favor, stood atop the Three Preceptors; in authority and office, he headed all chancellors. While the state survived he wavered in silence, holding office and eating salary without work; when the state perished he sought to preserve himself and escape harm, going out to meet and urge the new ruler's accession.
translations.idiomatic: Feng Dao, when honored, held the highest of the Three Preceptorships; when empowered, stood first among chancellors. While states endured he wavered in silence, drawing salary without doing his duty; when they fell he schemed for survival, greeting each conqueror and urging his accession.

sentences.zh: 君則興亡接踵，道則富貴自如，茲乃奸臣之尤，安得與他人為比哉！

translations.literal: Rulers rose and fell in succession, yet Dao's wealth and rank flowed on as before—this is the very extreme of treacherous ministers. How can he be compared with others!
translations.idiomatic: Dynasties rose and fell in turn while his wealth and rank never faltered—this is treachery at its worst. He cannot be compared with other compromised ministers.

sentences.zh: 或謂道能全身遠害於亂世，斯亦賢已。

translations.literal: Some say Dao was able to preserve his person and avoid harm in a chaotic age—this too is worthy.
translations.idiomatic: Some say Feng Dao preserved his life and kept clear of harm in a chaotic age—which makes him admirable.

sentences.zh: 臣謂君子有殺身成仁，無求生害仁，豈專以全身遠害為賢哉！

translations.literal: Your subject holds that the gentleman has giving up life to achieve benevolence; he has no seeking life to harm benevolence. How can preserving one's person and avoiding harm alone be deemed worthy!
translations.idiomatic: The noble man may die to fulfill his duty; he does not live at duty's expense. To call mere self-preservation in chaos wisdom is absurd.

sentences.zh: 然則盜跖病終而子路醢。

translations.literal: In that case, Robber Zhi died of illness while Zilu was minced.
translations.idiomatic: By that logic Robber Zhi died in bed while Zilu was butchered.

sentences.zh: 果誰賢乎？

translations.literal: In the end, which was the worthier?
translations.idiomatic: Which was truly the better man?

sentences.zh: 抑此非特道之愆也，時君亦有責焉，何則？

translations.literal: Yet this is not Feng Dao's fault alone—the rulers of the time also bear blame. Why is this?
translations.idiomatic: But this fault lies not with Feng Dao alone—the rulers of the age share the blame. Why?

sentences.zh: 不正之女，中士羞以為家；

translations.literal: A woman who is not chaste—men of the middle rank are ashamed to take her into the family;
translations.idiomatic: No decent man would take an improper woman into his house;

sentences.zh: 不忠之人，中君羞以為臣。

translations.literal: a man who is not loyal—a ruler of the middle rank is ashamed to make him a minister.
translations.idiomatic: no respectable ruler would appoint a disloyal man as minister.

sentences.zh: 彼相前朝，語其忠則反君事仇，語其智則社稷為墟。

translations.literal: That man had been chancellor of a former dynasty. Speak of his loyalty, and he turned on his ruler to serve his enemy; speak of his wisdom, and the altars of soil and grain became ruins.
translations.idiomatic: A man who had served a previous dynasty as chancellor—call him loyal and you must admit he betrayed his lord for his enemy; call him wise and you must admit he watched the altars of state crumble.

sentences.zh: 後來之君，不誅不棄，乃復用以為相，彼又安肯盡忠於我而能獲其用乎！

translations.literal: Yet the rulers who came after neither executed nor dismissed him, but again employed him as chancellor—how then could he whole-heartedly devote loyalty to them, and how could they gain his true service!
translations.idiomatic: Yet later rulers neither punished nor dismissed him, but made him chancellor again—how then could he serve them faithfully, or they expect loyalty from him?

sentences.zh: 故曰：非特道之愆，亦時君之責也！

translations.literal: Therefore it is said: this is not Feng Dao's fault alone—it is also the responsibility of the rulers of the time!
translations.idiomatic: As the saying goes: the blame falls not on Feng Dao alone, but on the rulers who employed him.

sentences.zh: 辛酉，符彥卿奏北漢憲州刺史太原韓光願、嵐州刺史郭言皆舉城降。

translations.literal: On xinyou, Fu Yanqing reported that Han Guangyuan, Prefect of Xian in Northern Han from Taiyuan, and Guo Yan, Prefect of Lan, had both surrendered their cities.
translations.idiomatic: On xinyou Fu Yanqing reported that Han Guangyuan, Northern Han prefect of Xian in Taiyuan, and Guo Yan, prefect of Lan, had surrendered their cities.

sentences.zh: 初，符彥卿有女適李守貞之子崇訓，相者言其貴當為天下母。

translations.literal: Earlier, Fu Yanqing had a daughter who married Li Shouzhen's son Chongxun. A physiognomist said her nobility would make her mother of the realm.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Yanqing had a daughter married to Li Shouzhen's son Chongxun. A fortune-teller said her destiny was to be mother to the realm.

sentences.zh: 守貞喜曰：「吾婦猶母天下，況我乎！」

translations.literal: Shouzhen rejoiced, saying, "If my daughter-in-law is yet to be mother of all under Heaven, how much more so am I!"
translations.idiomatic: Shouzhen exulted: "If my daughter-in-law is destined to mother the realm, how much greater must my own fate be!"

sentences.zh: 反意遂決。

translations.literal: His intention to rebel was thus settled.
translations.idiomatic: His decision to rebel was sealed.

sentences.zh: 及敗，崇訓先自刃其弟妹，次及符氏；

translations.literal: When he was defeated, Chongxun first himself slew his younger siblings, then turned to the Fu lady;
translations.idiomatic: When defeat came Chongxun first killed his younger siblings, then turned on Lady Fu;

sentences.zh: 符氏匿幃下，崇訓倉猝求之不獲，遂自剄。

translations.literal: Lady Fu hid beneath a curtain. Chongxun, in haste, searched for her but could not find her, and then cut his own throat.
translations.idiomatic: Lady Fu hid beneath a curtain. In his haste Chongxun could not find her and cut his own throat.

sentences.zh: 亂兵既入，符氏安坐堂上，叱亂兵曰：「吾父與郭公為昆弟，汝曹勿無禮！」

translations.literal: Once the disorderly troops had entered, Lady Fu sat calmly in the hall and shouted at them: "My father and Lord Guo are sworn brothers—do not be insolent!"
translations.idiomatic: When rebel soldiers burst in Lady Fu sat calmly in the hall and scolded them: "My father and Lord Guo are sworn brothers—you will show respect!"

sentences.zh: 太祖遣使歸之於彥卿。

translations.literal: Taizu dispatched messengers to return her to Yanqing.
translations.idiomatic: Taizu sent envoys to return her to Fu Yanqing.

sentences.zh: 及帝鎮澶州，太祖為帝娶之。

translations.literal: When the Emperor was Military Governor of Chanzhou, Taizu arranged for him to marry her.
translations.idiomatic: Later, when the Emperor governed Chanzhou, Taizu arranged their marriage.

sentences.zh: 壬戌，立為皇后。

translations.literal: On renxu, she was established as empress.
translations.idiomatic: On renxu she was made empress.

sentences.zh: 後性和惠而明決，帝甚重之。

translations.literal: The empress was by nature gentle and kind yet clear and resolute; the Emperor greatly valued her.
translations.idiomatic: Gentle and kind yet clear and decisive in counsel, she won the Emperor's deepest regard.

sentences.zh: 王彥超、韓通攻石州，克之，執刺史安彥進。

translations.literal: Wang Yanchao and Han Tong attacked Shizhou, captured it, and seized the Prefect An Yanjin.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Yanchao and Han Tong took Shizhou and captured its prefect An Yanjin.

sentences.zh: 癸亥，沁州刺史李廷誨降。

translations.literal: On guihai, Li Tinghui, Prefect of Qin, surrendered.
translations.idiomatic: On guihai Qin Prefecture's governor Li Tinghui surrendered.

sentences.zh: 庚午，帝發潞州，趣晉陽。

translations.literal: On gengwu, the Emperor departed from Luzhou and hastened toward Jinyang.
translations.idiomatic: On gengwu the Emperor marched from Luzhou toward Jinyang.

sentences.zh: 癸酉，北漢忻州監軍李勍殺刺史趙皋及契丹通事楊耨姑，舉城降。

translations.literal: On guiyou, Li Xiong, military supervisor of Xin Prefecture in Northern Han, killed the Prefect Zhao Gao and the Khitan liaison officer Yang Nougu, and surrendered the city.
translations.idiomatic: On guiyou Northern Han's Xin Prefecture supervisor Li Xiong killed the prefect Zhao Gao and the Khitan interpreter Yang Nougu and surrendered the city.

sentences.zh: 以勍為忻州刺史。

translations.literal: Li Xiong was appointed Prefect of Xin.
translations.idiomatic: Li Xiong was appointed prefect of Xin.

sentences.zh: 王逵表請復徙使府治朗州。

translations.literal: Wang Kui submitted a memorial requesting that the commissionerate headquarters be moved back to Lang Prefecture.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Kui memorialized to restore the commissionerate's seat at Langzhou.
